F1.quote: This interactive tool contains The Budget Lab's ongoing analysis of potential AI impacts on the labor market.
F1.claim: the tracker defined by its operator: an interactive tool holding the Lab's ongoing analysis of potential AI impacts on the labor market
F1.lineage: what it is: the Lab's ongoing tracker of AI's impact on the labor market

F2.quote: Tracking the Impact of AI on the Labor Market October 14, 2026 | Updated: October 14, 2026
F2.claim: the tracker's page, titled 'Tracking the Impact of AI on the Labor Market', dated and updated 14 October 2026

F3.quote: Copyright ©2026 Yale University. All rights reserved. The Budget Lab 127 Wall Street, New Haven, CT 06511
F3.claim: the page is The Budget Lab's, under Yale University's copyright, all rights reserved

F4.quote: Evaluating the Impact of AI on the Labor Market: Current State of Affairs Martha Gimbel , Molly Kinder , Joshua Kendall and Maddie Lee October 1, 2025
F4.claim: the first report: 'Evaluating the Impact of AI on the Labor Market: Current State of Affairs', by Martha Gimbel, Molly Kinder, Joshua Kendall and Maddie Lee, 1 October 2025
F4.lineage: the analysis it continues: the first report and its documentation

F5.quote: Martha Gimbel , Executive Director of the Budget Lab Molly Kinder , Senior Fellow – Brookings Metro Joshua Kendall , Research Fellow at the Budget Lab Maddie Lee , Research Assistant at the Budget Lab
F5.claim: the authors' positions: Gimbel the Lab's executive director, Kinder a senior fellow at Brookings Metro, Kendall and Lee of the Lab

F6.quote: While the occupational mix is changing more quickly than it has in the past, it is not a large difference and predates the widespread introduction of AI in the workforce.
F6.claim: October 2025: the occupational mix changing faster than in the past, by no large difference, and from before AI's widespread introduction

F7.quote: Currently, measures of exposure, automation, and augmentation show no sign of being related to changes in employment or unemployment.
F7.claim: October 2025: exposure, automation and augmentation measures show no sign of relation to employment or unemployment
F7.lineage: finding: exposure and usage against employment and unemployment

F8.quote: Better data is needed to fully understand the impact of AI on the labor market.
F8.claim: the report's stated need: better data to understand AI's labor-market impact fully
F8.lineage: usage data: its source, its reach and the data the Lab asks for

F9.quote: We plan on updating this analysis regularly moving forward to see how the impact of AI on the labor market changes over time.
F9.claim: October 2025: the plan to update the analysis regularly

F10.quote: We plan on updating this analysis regularly moving forward to see how the impact of AI on the labor market changes over time.
F10.claim: the tracker page carries the same plan to update regularly

F11.quote: First, is the pace of labor market change in this 33-month period of employment disruption different from past periods of early technological change? Second, is there evidence of economy-wide employment effects?
F11.claim: the report's two questions: whether labor-market change in 33 months differs from earlier technological change, and whether there are economy-wide employment effects
F11.lineage: method: occupational dissimilarity, and synthetic differences-in-differences

F12.quote: Overall, our metrics indicate that the broader labor market has not experienced a discernible disruption since ChatGPT’s release 33 months ago, undercutting fears that AI automation is currently eroding the demand for cognitive labor across the economy.
F12.claim: the report's headline: no discernible disruption of the broader labor market in the 33 months since ChatGPT's release

F13.quote: Of course, our analysis is not predictive of the future.
F13.claim: the report's limit: the analysis does not predict the future
F13.lineage: the limit: not yet, and the findings may change

F14.quote: We adapt Duncan and Duncan’s methodology to construct a dissimilarity index of the change in the occupational mix over time using monthly CPS data.
F14.claim: the churn measure: a dissimilarity index of the occupational mix over time, adapted from Duncan and Duncan, on monthly CPS data
F14.lineage: method: occupational dissimilarity, and synthetic differences-in-differences

F15.quote: Note that a change over this time period simply reflects change — it does not take a stance on the cause of that change.
F15.claim: the churn measure's own limit: it records change and takes no stance on its cause
F15.lineage: method: occupational dissimilarity, and synthetic differences-in-differences

F16.quote: Repeating this analysis by industry similarly suggests a limited effect of AI.
F16.claim: by industry the analysis suggests a limited effect of AI

F17.quote: If generative AI were in fact substantially changing the labor market for recent college graduates, we would expect to see a growing dissimilarity in the occupational mix between these two groups. … However, our results should be interpreted with caution particularly given small sample sizes.
F17.claim: recent graduates: a growing dissimilarity against older workers would be expected if AI were changing their market; the results are to be read with caution for small samples

F18.quote: The dissimilarity has increased slightly faster in recent months than it did in a previous time period, which could be consistent with a recent paper from Brynjolfsson et al. showing a possible impact of AI on employment of early career workers. It could also simply reflect a slowing labor market.
F18.claim: the graduates' dissimilarity rose slightly faster, possibly consistent with Brynjolfsson et al. or with a slowing labor market

F19.quote: This refers, generally, to whether utilizing ChatGPT4 technology can help reduce the time it takes to complete the occupation’s tasks by at least 50%.
F19.claim: the exposure measure used: OpenAI's, whether ChatGPT-4 technology can cut an occupation's task time by at least 50%
F19.lineage: exposure metrics: what they measure and what they do not

F20.quote: The share of workers in the lowest, middle, and highest occupational exposure groups stay stable at around 29%, 46% and 18%, respectively.
F20.claim: the shares of workers in low, middle and high exposure groups stable at about 29%, 46% and 18%
F20.lineage: finding: exposure and usage against employment and unemployment

F21.quote: Even when specifically examining the unemployed population, there is no clear growth in exposure to generative AI.
F21.claim: no clear growth in the generative-AI exposure of the unemployed
F21.lineage: finding: exposure and usage against employment and unemployment

F22.quote: Unfortunately, comprehensive usage data is not publicly available. The best available data we have is from OpenAI and Anthropic , respectively, that detail the occupations that are most “exposed” to genAI tools (a theoretical, forward-looking metric across all jobs) and that have the highest actual usage of one specific AI tool, Claude (a more narrow, present-focused metric).
F22.claim: the data providers: OpenAI for exposure (theoretical, forward-looking) and Anthropic for actual usage of one tool, Claude; comprehensive usage data is not public
F22.lineage: usage data: its source, its reach and the data the Lab asks for

F23.quote: Anthropic’s data on AI usage shows similar trends of stability over time, rather than disruption.
F23.claim: Anthropic's usage data shows stability over time, not disruption
F23.lineage: finding: exposure and usage against employment and unemployment

F24.quote: A key limitation of OpenAI’s “exposure” data is that it is not based on actual usage, and should therefore be interpreted as a theoretical estimate of the jobs and sectors that could , in theory, be impacted.
F24.claim: the exposure data's limit: not based on actual usage; a theoretical estimate of what could be impacted
F24.lineage: exposure metrics: what they measure and what they do not

F25.quote: Thus data from Claude usage alone is not representative of how workers across the economy are using AI chatbots and tools.
F25.claim: the usage data's limit: Claude usage alone does not represent how workers across the economy use AI tools
F25.lineage: usage data: its source, its reach and the data the Lab asks for

F26.quote: To accurately measure AI’s impact on the labor force, the most important data needed is comprehensive usage data from all the leading AI companies at the individual and enterprise level, including APIs.
F26.claim: the data the Lab asks for: comprehensive usage data from all the leading AI companies, individual and enterprise, APIs included
F26.lineage: usage data: its source, its reach and the data the Lab asks for

F27.quote: While anxiety over the effects of AI on today’s labor market is widespread, our data suggests it remains largely speculative.
F27.claim: the report's summary: widespread anxiety over AI's labor-market effects remains largely speculative on its data

F28.quote: While generative AI looks likely to join the ranks of transformative, general purpose technologies, it is too soon to tell how disruptive the technology will be to jobs.
F28.claim: too soon to tell how disruptive generative AI will be to jobs, though it looks likely to be a general purpose technology
F28.lineage: the limit: not yet, and the findings may change

F29.quote: The occupational mix is not yet changing in ways that clearly align with the introduction of AI into the workforce.
F29.claim: the tracker: the occupational mix is not yet changing in ways clearly aligned with AI's introduction

F30.quote: Measures of AI usage show no connection to changes in employment or unemployment.
F30.claim: the tracker: AI usage measures show no connection to changes in employment or unemployment
F30.lineage: finding: exposure and usage against employment and unemployment

F31.quote: A synthetic differences-in-differences analysis of AI exposure does not yet clearly indicate an AI-related labor market footprint.
F31.claim: the tracker: the synthetic differences-in-differences analysis does not yet clearly indicate an AI-related labor-market footprint
F31.lineage: finding: exposed against unexposed workers, employment and wages

F32.quote: Labor Market AI Exposure: What Do We Know? Martha Gimbel , Joshua Kendall and Ryan Kulsakdinun February 19, 2026
F32.claim: the exposure review: 'Labor Market AI Exposure: What Do We Know?', by Gimbel, Kendall and Kulsakdinun, 19 February 2026
F32.lineage: the analysis it continues: the first report and its documentation

F33.quote: AI exposure metrics broadly agree with each other, but that they disagree with each other more on highly exposed occupations. The key point of disagreement between different AI exposure metrics is in the magnitude of exposure, not whether an occupation is exposed.
F33.claim: exposure metrics broadly agree, disagree more on highly exposed occupations, and differ in magnitude more than in whether an occupation is exposed
F33.lineage: exposure metrics: what they measure and what they do not

F34.quote: Occupational exposure to AI is not indicative of a jobs AI will automate out of existence. Rather, it indicates places in the labor market where AI could have an impact.
F34.claim: the governing limit: exposure does not indicate jobs AI will automate away, only places where AI could have an impact
F34.lineage: exposure metrics: what they measure and what they do not

F35.quote: Many analysts—including those at The Budget Lab—utilize Eloundou et al.’s exposure metrics, which measure Generative AI’s (GenAI) ability to speed up work task completion.
F35.claim: the Lab among the analysts who use Eloundou et al.'s exposure metrics, which measure GenAI's ability to speed task completion
F35.lineage: exposure metrics: what they measure and what they do not

F36.quote: Microsoft researchers Tomlinson et al. (2025) created the ai_applicability_score. … They distinguish their work from other researchers by looking at individual conversations with Microsoft’s Copilot AI.
F36.claim: one of the seven metrics is Microsoft researchers' AI applicability score, built from individual Copilot conversations
F36.lineage: exposure metrics: what they measure and what they do not

F37.quote: This analysis is a reminder to be humble about how much we know about where AI disruption to the labor market could be going.
F37.claim: the review's limit: humility about where AI disruption of the labor market could go
F37.lineage: the limit: not yet, and the findings may change

F38.quote: AI Is Probably Not (Yet) the Reason for Labor Market Weakening Ryan Nunn May 7, 2026
F38.claim: the State of the Economy note: 'AI Is Probably Not (Yet) the Reason for Labor Market Weakening', Ryan Nunn, 7 May 2026

F39.quote: New Budget Lab research subjects the jobs data to an econometric method that makes AI-exposed and unexposed occupations comparable The results do not yet show clear indication of labor market effects of AI
F39.claim: the note: new research makes exposed and unexposed occupations comparable, and its results do not yet show clear labor-market effects of AI
F39.lineage: finding: exposed against unexposed workers, employment and wages

F40.quote: A relatively recent methodological innovation, called synthetic differences-in-differences, helps to distinguish any genuine impact of AI on exposed occupations from the persistent differences between exposed and unexposed jobs.
F40.claim: the method: synthetic differences-in-differences, separating a genuine AI impact on exposed occupations from persistent differences between exposed and unexposed jobs
F40.lineage: method: occupational dissimilarity, and synthetic differences-in-differences

F41.quote: The estimate is close to zero and cannot be distinguished from it, statistically speaking. The same is true for Figure 2, which shows impacts on inflation-adjusted hourly wages.
F41.claim: the estimates for employment in the average exposed occupation and for inflation-adjusted hourly wages are close to zero and statistically indistinguishable from it
F41.lineage: finding: exposed against unexposed workers, employment and wages

F42.quote: From its post-pandemic low of 3.4% in April 2023, the unemployment rate has risen to 4.3% in March 2026—a higher though still healthy level. Both layoffs and hires have been low, with unemployed job seekers having an especially difficult and worsening experience.
F42.claim: the market around it: unemployment from 3.4% (April 2023) to 4.3% (March 2026), low layoffs and low hires, a worsening experience for the unemployed

F43.quote: many have suspected that it bears the imprint of widespread AI adoption by employers. … However, the weight of the evidence—to date—does not support this conjecture.
F43.claim: the conjecture that the cooled market bears the imprint of employers' AI adoption is not supported by the weight of the evidence to date

F44.quote: One feature of that previous analysis is that it does not rely on AI exposure metrics and is not subject to critiques of those measures. However, it does not formally attempt to identify effects of AI.
F44.claim: the churn analysis: free of exposure metrics and their critiques, and not a formal attempt to identify AI's effects
F44.lineage: method: occupational dissimilarity, and synthetic differences-in-differences

F45.quote: AI seems quite likely to eventually leave its mark on the labor market, even if it has not already.
F45.claim: the Lab's expectation: AI quite likely to leave its mark on the labor market eventually, even if not already
F45.lineage: the limit: not yet, and the findings may change

F46.quote: A principal reason for this low growth is the slowdown in net immigration, which reduced labor force growth.
F46.claim: a principal reason for low payroll growth: the slowdown in net immigration

F47.quote: Yale Budget Lab Executive Director Martha Gimbel on why AI hasn't disrupted ...
F47.claim: a Quest Means Business video (5:33) in which the Lab's executive director speaks on why AI hasn't disrupted (the title truncated)
F47.checked_against: card title (unreachable card; no snippet on the rail)

F48.claim: the tracker published 16 July 2026, updated 15 September 2026

F50.quote: The Budget Lab's labor market analysis, updated to incorporate August 2026 CPS microdata, does not provide clear evidence of labor market disruption associated with AI. Churn across occupations, AI exposure among the unemployed, and usage data all remain flat, lie within historical ranges, or continue along pre-AI trends.
F50.claim: the September 2026 update, on August 2026 CPS microdata: no clear evidence of AI-associated disruption; churn, exposure among the unemployed and usage data flat, within historical ranges or on pre-AI trends

F51.quote: Of course, these findings may change as new data become available. The Budget Lab plans to continue monitoring AI-relevant trends to assess how job impacts might change.
F51.claim: the tracker's stated limit: the findings may change with new data; monitoring continues
F51.lineage: the limit: not yet, and the findings may change

F52.quote: Major categories of analysis can be accessed by clicking tabs towards the top of the page with the following names: Occupational churn, AI metrics, and Comparisons of AI-exposed and unexposed workers.
F52.claim: three sections: occupational churn, AI metrics, comparisons of AI-exposed and unexposed workers
F52.lineage: the unit: three sections on monthly CPS data

F53.quote: Occupational churn, AI-exposure rates of the unemployed, and related analysis can be found in Gimbel et al. (2025). Details of AI exposure metrics are discussed in Gimbel, Kendall, and Kulsakdinun (2026).
F53.claim: its documentation: Gimbel et al. (2025) for churn and the exposure of the unemployed; Gimbel, Kendall and Kulsakdinun (2026) for the exposure metrics
F53.lineage: the analysis it continues: the first report and its documentation

F54.claim: the tracker's data downloadable ('Download All Data')
